items.readable_text:
Content:
We know how to find a Fourier-series particular solution [MATH: y_p] for a periodically forced linear ODE.
In this topic, the new step is how to use [MATH: y_p] to satisfy an initial condition.

Content:
Recall that once a particular solution [MATH: y_p] is chosen, the full solution has the form
[MATH: y = y_c + y_p,]
where [MATH: y_c] solves the corresponding homogeneous equation.

Content:
Now, suppose the IVP is given at [MATH: x=x_0{:}]
[MATH: y(x_0)=y_0.]
Then,
[MATH: y_0 = y_c(x_0)+y_p(x_0).]

Content:
A useful simplification is to choose the particular solution so that
[MATH: y_p(x_0)=0.]
In that case, the initial condition becomes
[MATH: y_0 = y_c(x_0),]
so we can solve for the constant(s) in [MATH: y_c] immediately (without evaluating any Fourier sums at [MATH: x_0]).

Content:
On the next slide, we’ll apply this idea in an example.

items.readable_text:
Content:
For example, consider the initial value problem
[MATH: y'-2y = f(x), \qquad y(0)=3,]
where [MATH: f(x)] is a [MATH: 2]-periodic function. Suppose we choose the forcing (and hence the Fourier-series particular solution) so that
[MATH: y_p(0)=0.]

Content:
First, solve the homogeneous equation:
[MATH: y' - 2y = 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
y_c = Ae^{2x}.]

Content:
A [MATH: 2]-periodic forcing function can be written using harmonics of frequency [MATH: \pi], so we may write the particular solution in the form
[MATH: y_p(x)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(a_n\cos(n\pi x)+b_n\sin(n\pi x)\right).]
Thus the full solution is
[MATH: y(x)=Ae^{2x}+\sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(a_n\cos(n\pi x)+b_n\sin(n\pi x)\right).]

Content:
Now apply [MATH: y(0)=3] and use [MATH: y_p(0)=0]:
[MATH: y(0)|= Ae^{2(0)} + y_{p}(0); 3|= A(1) + 0; A|= 3.]

Content:
Therefore,
[MATH: y(x)=
3e^{2x}+\sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(a_n\cos(n\pi x)+b_n\sin(n\pi x)\right).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form [MATH: y' + P(x)y = f(x)] is given by [MATH: y = y_c + y_p,] where [MATH: y_c] is the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and [MATH: y_p] is a particular solution.

First, we find the homogeneous solution. The general solution of [MATH: y' - 6y = 0] is [MATH: y_c = Ae^{6x},] where [MATH: A] is an arbitrary constant.

Next, we identify the form of the general solution. Because the operator [MATH: y' - 6y] involves a first derivative, a periodic forcing function [MATH: f(x)] results in a particular solution containing both sine and cosine terms: [MATH: y(x) \sim Ae^{6x} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty (a_n \cos(n\pi x) + b_n \sin(n\pi x))]

Now, we apply the initial condition [MATH: y(1)=4.] Using the hint that the particular solution part evaluates to zero at [MATH: x=1,] we have [MATH: y(1)|= Ae^{6(1)} + y_{p}(1); 4|= Ae^{6} + 0; A|= 4e^{− 6}.]

Finally, we substitute [MATH: A] back into the homogeneous part: [MATH: y_c = (4e^{-6})e^{6x} = 4e^{6x-6}]

Therefore, the solution is [MATH: y(x) \sim \bbox[4pt,border: 0.5px solid black]{4e^{6x-6}} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty (a_n \cos(n\pi x) + b_n \sin(n\pi x)).]

items.title: Second-Order IVPs

sections.normalized_html: When we solve a second-order IVP using Fourier series, we still represent the solution in the form [MATH: y = y_c + y_p,] but since the homogeneous solution has two constants, we use two conditions: [MATH: y(0)=y_0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad y'(0)=y_1]
sections.readable_text:
When we solve a second-order IVP using Fourier series, we still represent the solution in the form
[MATH: y = y_c + y_p,]
but since the homogeneous solution has two constants, we use two conditions:
[MATH: y(0)=y_0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y'(0)=y_1]

sections.normalized_html: Before we start, we can use the forcing series properties to simplify our work. For a second-order equation of the form [MATH: y'' + \omega^2 y = f(x)] with no [MATH: y'] (damping) term, the particular solution can be simplified. Here, we have two cases:
sections.readable_text:
Before we start, we can use the forcing series properties to simplify our work. For a second-order equation of the form
[MATH: y'' + \omega^2 y = f(x)]
with no [MATH: y'] (damping) term, the particular solution can be simplified. Here, we have two cases:

sections.normalized_html:
• Case 1: [MATH: f(x)] is odd.

    If [MATH: f(x)] is odd and the equation has the form [MATH: y''+\omega^2 y=f(x)], then the particular solution is also odd, so it is a sine series: [MATH: y_p(x)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right)] This immediately gives [MATH: y_p(0)=0,] so the condition [MATH: y(0)=y_0] determines the cosine constant in [MATH: y_c] without evaluating any infinite sum at [MATH: 0].

  • Case 2: [MATH: f(x)] is even.

    If [MATH: f(x)] is even and the equation has the form [MATH: y''+\omega^2 y=f(x)], then the particular solution is also even, so it is a cosine series: [MATH: y_p(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right)] Here, the derivative is a sine series: [MATH: y_p'(x)=-\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{a_n n\pi}{L} \sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right)] This immediately gives [MATH: y_p'(0)=0,] so the condition [MATH: y'(0)=y_1] determines the sine constant in [MATH: y_c] without evaluating any infinite sum at [MATH: 0].

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We know how to find a Fourier-series particular solution [MATH: y_p] for a periodically forced linear ODE.
In this topic, the new step is how to use [MATH: y_p] to satisfy an initial condition.

Content:
Recall that once a particular solution [MATH: y_p] is chosen, the full solution has the form
[MATH: y = y_c + y_p,]
where [MATH: y_c] solves the corresponding homogeneous equation.

Content:
Now, suppose the IVP is given at [MATH: x=x_0{:}]
[MATH: y(x_0)=y_0.]
Then,
[MATH: y_0 = y_c(x_0)+y_p(x_0).]

Content:
A useful simplification is to choose the particular solution so that
[MATH: y_p(x_0)=0.]
In that case, the initial condition becomes
[MATH: y_0 = y_c(x_0),]
so we can solve for the constant(s) in [MATH: y_c] immediately (without evaluating any Fourier sums at [MATH: x_0]).

Content:
On the next slide, we’ll apply this idea in an example.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: A Worked Example

Content:
For example, consider the initial value problem
[MATH: y'-2y = f(x), \qquad y(0)=3,]
where [MATH: f(x)] is a [MATH: 2]-periodic function. Suppose we choose the forcing (and hence the Fourier-series particular solution) so that
[MATH: y_p(0)=0.]

Content:
First, solve the homogeneous equation:
[MATH: y' - 2y = 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
y_c = Ae^{2x}.]

Content:
A [MATH: 2]-periodic forcing function can be written using harmonics of frequency [MATH: \pi], so we may write the particular solution in the form
[MATH: y_p(x)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(a_n\cos(n\pi x)+b_n\sin(n\pi x)\right).]
Thus the full solution is
[MATH: y(x)=Ae^{2x}+\sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(a_n\cos(n\pi x)+b_n\sin(n\pi x)\right).]

Content:
Now apply [MATH: y(0)=3] and use [MATH: y_p(0)=0]:
[MATH: y(0)|= Ae^{2(0)} + y_{p}(0); 3|= A(1) + 0; A|= 3.]

Content:
Therefore,
[MATH: y(x)=
3e^{2x}+\sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(a_n\cos(n\pi x)+b_n\sin(n\pi x)\right).]

---

Item 3 — Example: Solving First-Order IVPs Using Fourier Series

Example Prompt:
Consider the initial value problem
[MATH: y'-6y = f(x), \qquad y(1)=4]
where [MATH: f(x)] is a [MATH: 2]-periodic function. Fill in the missing part in the solution of the IVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution [MATH: y_p] of the differential equation.

Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function [MATH: f(x)] is chosen such that the particular solution [MATH: y_p] satisfies [MATH: y_p(1)=0.]

[MATH: AAA?AAA]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form [MATH: y' + P(x)y = f(x)] is given by
[MATH: y = y_c + y_p,]
where [MATH: y_c] is the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and [MATH: y_p] is a particular solution.

First, we find the homogeneous solution. The general solution of [MATH: y' - 6y = 0] is
[MATH: y_c = Ae^{6x},]
where [MATH: A] is an arbitrary constant.

Next, we identify the form of the general solution. Because the operator [MATH: y' - 6y] involves a first derivative, a periodic forcing function [MATH: f(x)] results in a particular solution containing both sine and cosine terms:
[MATH: y(x) \sim Ae^{6x} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty (a_n \cos(n\pi x) + b_n \sin(n\pi x))]

Now, we apply the initial condition [MATH: y(1)=4.] Using the hint that the particular solution part evaluates to zero at [MATH: x=1,] we have
[MATH: y(1)|= Ae^{6(1)} + y_{p}(1); 4|= Ae^{6} + 0; A|= 4e^{− 6}.]

Finally, we substitute [MATH: A] back into the homogeneous part:
[MATH: y_c = (4e^{-6})e^{6x} = 4e^{6x-6}]

Therefore, the solution is
[MATH: y(x) \sim
\bbox[4pt,border: 0.5px solid black]{4e^{6x-6}} +
\sum_{n=1}^\infty (a_n \cos(n\pi x) + b_n \sin(n\pi x)).]

Item 6 — Tutorial: Second-Order IVPs

Content:
When we solve a second-order IVP using Fourier series, we still represent the solution in the form
[MATH: y = y_c + y_p,]
but since the homogeneous solution has two constants, we use two conditions:
[MATH: y(0)=y_0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y'(0)=y_1]

Content:
Before we start, we can use the forcing series properties to simplify our work. For a second-order equation of the form
[MATH: y'' + \omega^2 y = f(x)]
with no [MATH: y'] (damping) term, the particular solution can be simplified. Here, we have two cases:

Content:
- Case 1: [MATH: f(x)] is odd.

If [MATH: f(x)] is odd and the equation has the form [MATH: y''+\omega^2 y=f(x)], then the particular solution is also odd, so it is a sine series:
[MATH: y_p(x)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right)]
This immediately gives [MATH: y_p(0)=0,] so the condition [MATH: y(0)=y_0] determines the cosine constant in [MATH: y_c] without evaluating any infinite sum at [MATH: 0].
- Case 2: [MATH: f(x)] is even.

If [MATH: f(x)] is even and the equation has the form [MATH: y''+\omega^2 y=f(x)], then the particular solution is also even, so it is a cosine series:
[MATH: y_p(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right)]
Here, the derivative is a sine series:
[MATH: y_p'(x)=-\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{a_n n\pi}{L} \sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right)]
This immediately gives [MATH: y_p'(0)=0,] so the condition [MATH: y'(0)=y_1] determines the sine constant in [MATH: y_c] without evaluating any infinite sum at [MATH: 0].

Content:
In both cases, the key idea is that evaluating at [MATH: x=0] (and differentiating once) lets the initial conditions pick off the constants in [MATH: y_c] as cleanly as possible.

Content:
Let's see how this works in practice on the next slide.

---

Item 7 — Tutorial: A Worked Example of a Second-Order IVP

Content:
Consider the initial value problem
[MATH: y''+ 7y = f(x), \qquad y(0)=3,\quad y'(0)=0]
where [MATH: f(x)] is an even, [MATH: 2\pi]-periodic function. Since the forcing is even and the differential operator contains no [MATH: y'] term, we represent the particular solution as a cosine series:
[MATH: y_p(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n\cos(nx)]

Content:
Next, we solve the homogeneous equation [MATH: y''+7y=0.] The characteristic equation is [MATH: \lambda^2+7=0,] so

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form [MATH: y'' + \omega^2 y = f(x)] is given by [MATH: y = y_c + y_p,] where [MATH: y_c] is the solution to the homogeneous equation and [MATH: y_p] is a particular solution.

First, we address the particular solution [MATH: y_p.] Since [MATH: f(x)] is an odd function, its Fourier series consists only of sine terms. For a second-order equation with no [MATH: y'] (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an odd function. This is represented by the term
[MATH: y_p(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty
\dfrac{16(-1)^n}{n^2\pi^3\left(28-n^2\right)} \sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right).]

Next, we find the homogeneous solution. The characteristic equation [MATH: \lambda^2 + 7\pi^2 = 0] gives roots [MATH: \lambda = \pm \sqrt{7}\pi \textrm i.] So, we have
[MATH: y_c = A\cos(\sqrt{7}\pi x) + B\sin(\sqrt{7}\pi x).]

To find the unknown constants, we apply the initial conditions. Using [MATH: y(0)=0{:}]
[MATH: y(0)|= A\cos (0) + B\sin (0) + y_{p}(0); 0|= A(1) + 0 + 0; A|= 0]
Note that [MATH: y_p(0)=0] because the particular solution is a sine series.

Next, we use the derivative condition [MATH: y'(0)=0.] First, we compute the derivative of the total solution (with [MATH: A=0]):
[MATH: y'(x) \sim B(\sqrt{7}\pi)\cos(\sqrt{7}\pi x) + \sum_{n=1}^\infty
\dfrac{8(-1)^n}{n\pi^2\left(28-n^2\right)} \cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right)]

Applying [MATH: y'(0)=0] and noting that [MATH: \cos(0)=1,] we have
[MATH: 0|= B(sqrt(7)π) + ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(8(− 1)^{n})/(nπ^{2}(28 − n^{2})); B(sqrt(7)π)|= − ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(8(− 1)^{n})/(nπ^{2}(28 − n^{2})); B|= − (1)/(sqrt(7)π)∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(8(− 1)^{n})/(nπ^{2}(28 − n^{2})); = − ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(8(− 1)^{n})/(sqrt(7)nπ^{3}(28 − n^{2})).]

Substituting [MATH: B] back into [MATH: y_c = B\sin(\sqrt{7}\pi x),] we find the missing part:
[MATH: y(x)\sim
\bbox[4pt,border: 0.5px solid black]{-\sin(\sqrt{7}\pi x)\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{8(-1)^n}{\sqrt{7}n\pi^3\left(28-n^2\right)}}
+ \sum_{n=1}^\infty
\dfrac{16(-1)^n}{n^2\pi^3\left(28-n^2\right)} \sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right)]
